Timon
TY-mon
proper noun (person)
Greek Timon, "honorable, esteemed"; one of the seven men chosen to serve tables in Acts 6.

📖 Biblical Definition

Timon was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily ministration to the widows (Acts 6:5). His name means "honorable," and though Scripture records nothing of him beyond his place in the list, his appointment shines with quiet dignity. The Seven were the church's answer to a real and pressing need — the danger that, as the number of disciples multiplied, some of the needy would be overlooked. By appointing honorable, Spirit-filled men to this service, the apostles ensured that the practical love of the church would not fail. It is striking that two of the Seven, Stephen and Philip, soon appear as a mighty witness and an evangelist; the diaconate did not confine its members to tables alone, but the faithful discharge of humble service became the seedbed of wider usefulness. Of Timon himself nothing more is known, yet his name is preserved forever in the inspired record. Timon stands in the dictionary as one of the Seven whose name God saw fit to record, a witness that faithful service in the church, however obscure, is honorable in the sight of God, who forgets no labor of love done for His people in His name.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

One of the seven men chosen in Acts 6:5 to serve the widows; his name means "honorable," and though Scripture records no more of him, his place in the inspired list witnesses that obscure, faithful service is honorable before God.

TIMON, proper noun. "Honorable"; one of the seven men chosen to serve tables (Acts 6:5).

Appointed to the daily ministration to the widows.

Named only in the list of the Seven, yet preserved forever in Scripture.

Part of the office from which Stephen and Philip rose to wider witness.

A witness that obscure, faithful service is honorable before God.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 6:5 — "...and they chose Stephen... and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas a proselyte of Antioch:"

Heb 6:10 — "For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister."

Matt 25:40 — "...Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me."

1 Cor 4:2 — "Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Timon honors the recovery of the honor of obscure, faithful service, against a fame-seeking spirit that despises any ministry the world will not notice or applaud.

expand to see more

Obscurity-despised correction. A culture obsessed with recognition counts unnoticed service worthless. Timon is named once and never described, yet his name stands forever in the Word of God, and his service to the widows was dear to the Lord. The dictionary holds that God is not unrighteous to forget the labor of love shown toward His name (Heb 6:10); the obscure servant is seen, remembered, and honored by the One whose esteem outweighs all the applause of men.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithfulness in small and hidden things. It is required of stewards that they be found faithful (1 Cor 4:2), not famous. The dictionary commends the example of the lesser-known of the Seven: the kingdom of God advances through multitudes of faithful, unremembered servants, and what is done for the least of Christ's brethren is done unto Him (Matt 25:40), and shall not lose its reward.
